subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Comparing writers' ideas and perspectives across texts
Vocabulary, sentence structure and technical accuracy

questions.q: Paper 2 of the Edexcel GCSE English Language course focuses on non-fiction texts from which time periods?
questions.explain: Paper 2 pairs a 20th-century non-fiction text with a 21st-century one, whereas Paper 1 uses 19th-century fiction.

questions.q: What best defines non-fiction writing?
options: Writing based on real people, events, facts and opinions
Writing that is entirely invented by the author
Writing that always uses rhyme and rhythm
Writing that must be set in the past
questions.explain: Non-fiction deals with real subject matter, such as articles, letters, speeches, reviews and reports.

questions.q: In Section A of Paper 2, the two non-fiction texts are always...
options: Thematically linked so they can be compared
questions.explain: The paired texts share a theme, allowing candidates to compare the writers' ideas and perspectives.

questions.q: In the persuasive-technique mnemonic DAFOREST, the letter 'S' most commonly stands for...
questions.explain: DAFOREST covers Direct address, Alliteration, Facts, Opinion, Rhetorical questions, Emotive language, Statistics and Triplets.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a transactional writing form?
questions.explain: Transactional writing includes real-world non-fiction forms such as letters, articles, speeches, reports and reviews.

questions.q: Assessment Objective 6 (AO6) in the writing section mainly rewards...
options: Accurate spelling, punctuation and a range of sentence structures
Analysing a writer's use of imagery
questions.explain: AO6 assesses technical accuracy and the range of vocabulary and sentence structures used for effect.

questions.q: If a formal letter opens with 'Dear Sir or Madam', the correct sign-off is...
questions.explain: 'Yours faithfully' is used when the recipient's name is unknown; 'Yours sincerely' is used when it is known.

questions.q: Before planning a piece of transactional writing, candidates are advised to identify the purpose, audience and...
questions.explain: Purpose, Audience and Form (PAF) shape the register, structure and conventions a candidate should use.

questions.q: A writer states, 'This is the greatest injustice of our age.' This is best described as...
questions.explain: It expresses a personal judgement that cannot be proven, so it is an opinion rather than a verifiable fact.

questions.q: Identifying 'implicit' information in a text means...
options: Working out ideas that are suggested but not directly stated
Copying words directly from the text
Counting how many paragraphs there are
questions.explain: Implicit meaning is inferred from clues in the text, whereas explicit information is stated openly.

questions.q: When comparing two non-fiction texts, a strong answer focuses mainly on...
options: The writers' differing ideas and perspectives and how they are conveyed
The number of paragraphs in each
The names of the two authors
questions.explain: Comparison (AO3) rewards analysis of how each writer presents their viewpoint, not surface features.

questions.q: A writer describes pollution as 'a silent killer creeping through our cities.' The main technique used is...
questions.explain: Pollution is described as a 'killer' without using 'like' or 'as', making it a metaphor.

questions.q: Why might a writer use direct address ('you') in a persuasive article?
options: To make readers feel personally involved and responsible
To make the text more difficult to read
questions.explain: Direct address engages readers by speaking to them personally, increasing the persuasive impact.

questions.q: Which sign-off matches a letter beginning 'Dear Mrs Patel'?
questions.explain: When the recipient is named, 'Yours sincerely' is the correct formal closing.

questions.q: Using a deliberate short, one-word sentence for emphasis is an example of...
questions.explain: Controlled sentence variety, including short punchy sentences, is rewarded under AO6 as crafting for effect.

questions.q: The tone of a letter of complaint to a company should usually be...
questions.explain: A complaint is most effective when it stays formal and controlled while clearly stating the problem.

questions.q: You are asked to write a speech persuading students to recycle. Which opening is most appropriate?
options: Imagine a school buried under its own waste — that future is closer than you think.
Once upon a time there lived a lonely dragon.
Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to complain.
questions.explain: A speech should hook the audience with direct, persuasive language suited to its purpose and listeners.

questions.q: A task asks for a formal article for a broadsheet newspaper. Which sentence best fits the register?
options: Recent research suggests that screen time is reshaping how young people concentrate.
OMG screens are literally frying our brains lol.
Once, in a galaxy far away, there were no phones.
questions.explain: A broadsheet article needs a measured, formal register with standard English, not slang or letter conventions.

questions.q: A question asks you to 'support your answer with evidence from the text.' The best approach is to...
options: Make a point and back it up with a short quotation
Give your own personal story instead
Summarise the whole text with no quotations
Write about a different text you have read
questions.explain: Reading answers require points supported by precise textual references, in line with AO1 and AO2.

questions.q: To structure a comparison of two texts effectively, a useful method is to...
options: Discuss a shared idea, then show how each writer presents it differently
Write everything about Text 1, then everything unrelated about Text 2
questions.explain: Integrating both texts around shared ideas produces a genuine comparison rather than two separate accounts.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE English Language (1EN0) specification; Paper 2: Non-fiction and Transactional Writing
